verdicts.reason: X requires a focused modification to be proposed on top of the concession, while Y scores pure acknowledgment-and-weighing of a tradeoff even with no modification offered.
Both score whether specific affected or vulnerable groups and their concrete exposure are named versus generic appeals to the public or fairness.

X scores drafting-level specification of the requested change, while Y requires implementation analysis (who carries it out, what constraints bind), so exact rule text with no implementer analysis splits the two.

X rewards coordination design with other programs and systems to avoid duplication, while Y rewards locating a concrete legal or programmatic conflict and resolving it; a pure statutory-conflict argument or a pure data-sharing suggestion scores unevenly.

X scores a proposed monitoring or verification regime for the rule's functioning, while Y scores converting an ambiguous term into an operational definition; a comment can do either without the other.
Both score how fully a proposed alternative's mechanism is specified in the text itself, with the same failure mode of an alternative named but not described.
Both ask whether a concrete alternative regulatory design is offered in implementable detail, with identical zero anchors of mere objection.
First-hand operational practice and emotional intensity are unrelated dimensions; an outraged non-practitioner scores high on Y and zero on X.
X requires a remedy targeted to the mechanism as a scored component, while Y scores the causal tracing alone, so a mechanism-only diagnosis splits them.
Y scores only the causal chain from action to claimed outcome, whereas X additionally demands a remedy aimed at that mechanism.

X scores the concreteness of an offered alternative, while Y requires engagement with an opposing consideration or preservation of part of the proposal; a one-sided but fully specified alternative diverges.
Y scores reasoning about how the rule functions in practice even with no fix proposed, while X requires a workable adjustment plus identification of the implementer.
Both measure whether the comment fastens on identifiable provisions with issue-specific content versus generic text that could apply to any rule.
X rewards concrete situated observations paired with a role, while Y explicitly withholds credit for narrated experience unless generalized to a recurring problem and rule-level implication.
Designing a workable implementation adjustment and designing measurement or verification of performance are distinct asks that commonly appear separately.
X scores contribution of information not already in the record, while Y scores provision-specific reasoning; a well-targeted comment adding nothing new scores high on Y and low on X.
Citation of CFR part and section is a formal marker, whereas an ultra vires statutory-authority argument is a substantive legal claim that can appear with or without citations.
X credits any clearly named action the agency should take, while Y demands an identified provision plus drop-in text or a specific number, a far stricter bar.
Both score genuine engagement with the strongest countervailing consideration against the comment's own position, and both discount ritual or passing acknowledgment.
X measures textual coherence and absence of non-sequiturs, while Y measures substantive legal-technical analysis; the shared word 'coherence' names different things.
Y credits accurate targeted engagement with provisions generally, while X requires exact substitute language or a numeric threshold, so reasoned criticism without proposed text splits them.
Specificity of engagement with the proposal and contribution of decision-relevant new information are separable; a precise comment can add nothing the agency did not already have.
Both score whether a concrete, implementable alternative is described in enough detail to act on, with the same zero anchor of bare demand or rejection.
Proposing monitoring and verification machinery is unrelated to identifying and resolving conflicts with existing law and programs.

X rewards identifying a specific legal conflict or inconsistency and reasoning through it, while Y rewards administrability of the recommendation (a clear decision rule, threshold, or authority link).
Both score explicit comparison of plausible options with their costs and benefits and a reasoned preference, with the same zero anchor of a categorical endorsement.
Both score whether the commenter supplies its own numeric compliance-cost figures with the basis stated.
Identifying which groups bear costs is a distributional question, while spillovers across connected systems and sectors is a scope question that need not name any group.
X scores whether the request fits the agency's authority and this docket, while Y scores pinpointed engagement with a named provision plus a reason; either can be satisfied alone.
Both score whether factual claims are backed by identifiable, checkable evidence rather than assertion or slogan, and both attend to whether the support actually bears the claim.
Both score the level of mechanism detail in a proposed alternative, distinguishing a described, workable design from an alternative gestured at in name only.
X scores only whether criticism is aimed at the rule rather than at persons, while Y additionally penalizes any off-topic drift, so an unrelated but civil political digression diverges.
Both score whether an explicit, stepwise causal chain connects the rule to the claimed outcome rather than an asserted consequence.
Both require the comment to identify a particular provision or alternative and attach substantive reasoning to it, with generic subject-matter commentary scoring zero.
X scores only whether a clear action is asked of the agency, while Y scores accurate engagement with particular provisions; a specific ask with no provision-level engagement diverges.
Proposing exact substitute text or a threshold edit differs from supplying numbers that establish the magnitude of the underlying problem.

Both concern workable change, but X gates on implementation analysis (who implements, what constraints bind) while Y gates on the concreteness of an alternative design, so a well-specified alternative with no implementer analysis splits them.
Specifying a monitoring and correction loop differs from operationalizing an ambiguous definition into a testable rule.
Monitoring design is one narrow content type, while proposal-specific engagement is a general specificity criterion that most targeted comments satisfy without any monitoring proposal.
Both score whether important factual claims rest on identifiable, traceable sources rather than unsupported or self-evident assertion.
X is satisfied by pinpointing a provision and saying what is wrong with it, while Y additionally requires exact replacement language or a specific number.
Accurately characterizing the proposal is a comprehension criterion that a comment can meet without ever fastening on a named provision, which is what X requires.
X requires weighing multiple options against one another, while Y requires only one concrete implementable alternative with no comparison.
Both score whether claims are attached to identifiable, authoritative sources that support them, with unsupported assertion as the zero anchor.
Both score whether a specific mechanism is traced from the rule to concrete consequences rather than asserting that something is good or harmful.
Both require identifiable provisions to be targeted and supported with issue-specific reasoning, scoring generic or unexplained submissions at zero.
X credits any causal chain to the claimed outcome, while Y specifically credits reasoning about practical operation (workload, timing, ripple effects) for those carrying out the rule.
X scores whether the proposal is read and characterized correctly, while Y scores provision-level targeting with recommendations; an accurate but general response splits them.
Both score whether factual claims are tied to named, checkable sources that genuinely support the proposition, against vague or unattributed sourcing.
Refuting a specific premise the proposal rests on is narrower and distinct from the general requirement of pinpointing a provision and giving a reason.
X scores demonstrated knowledge of how the work is actually done in evaluating feasibility, while Y scores the design of a workable adjustment naming implementers and constraints.
Both score whether delayed, repeated, or cumulative effects over a stated horizon are analyzed rather than only immediate impacts.
X keys on conflicts, gaps, or overlaps with outside law and programs plus a proposed resolution, while Y also covers internal assumptions and inconsistencies with no external authority in play.
Contributing information new to the record is unrelated to conceding an opposing point and proposing a focused modification.
Both score whether the comment articulates the intermediate mechanism from the requirement to its concrete consequence rather than asserting the consequence.
X requires comparing alternatives against one another, while Y is satisfied by conceding a cost of the comment's own position with no alternative compared.
Both score whether the comment specifies what should be monitored, tested, or reported and how that information would reveal or correct performance.
Both score whether factual claims are attached to identifiable, authoritative, checkable sources rather than vague or unattributed backing.
X requires an explicit comparison of policy options with their costs and risks, while Y credits acknowledging a single countervailing cost to one's own recommendation.
Both score the particularity and checkability of the writer's own situated account (named place, date, incident, or caseload) against generic expressions of concern.
